title: How Does It Make Money?
goal: Your kid finds out how something free or cheap really pays for itself. They pick a free game, a video site, a museum or a day out, collect real evidence like counted ads, receipts and what's sold at the exit, estimate the money with simple math, draw a one-page money map, then plan how an idea of their own would make money.
need: One free or cheap thing your kid uses: a free game or app, a video site, a museum or a day out
Your phone or tablet for the screen version, with purchases locked
Receipts, a price list or a map from a day out
A timer, paper and coloured pencils

academics.subject: Math
academics.text: multiplying people by what each spends

academics.subject: Data

academics.subject: Economics
academics.text: the different ways a business earns

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Kids assume free means nobody pays. Hold back the answer and play detective alongside them: you hold the device and the wallet, they hold the tally, and every arrow on the money map has to point to something you both saw.

plan.what: Pick it and write the first guess (Step 1).
Estimate, map and plan your own (Steps 3 to 5).

troubleshoot.q: They want to buy something in the game
troubleshoot.a: Agree before you start that this is a detective visit, not a shopping trip. They write the price in the tally instead. Counting it is the job.

troubleshoot.q: We can't find how much it earns
troubleshoot.a: Companies rarely say, and small places almost never do. A clear estimate is the goal, not the right answer. Ask which number would change their guess most.

troubleshoot.q: It has no ads and costs nothing
troubleshoot.a: A great case. Look for the other payers: taxes for a library or park, donations, members, or a sponsor's name on a sign.

lesson.text: Almost nothing is free to run. When the person using it doesn't pay, someone else does: companies paying for ads to reach you, a few players buying extras, or visitors paying for food, parking and the shop on the way out.
lesson.before: 'It's free, so it doesn't make money.'

model.line: 4 ads in 10 minutes of a free game, plus a 30-second ad for an extra life.
Coin packs from $0.99, and $4.99 to switch the ads off.
The 980 who never pay still earn it money, by watching the ads.

lesson.modelNote: 'Free' was where the first guess stopped. Ten minutes of counting found two kinds of payer: companies buying the players' attention with ads, and a few players buying their way past them.

steps.title: Pick it and guess
steps.why: A guess written down first makes the evidence surprising.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one free or cheap thing they use, like a free game, a video site, a free museum or a zoo, and writes their guess: who pays for it? Then they read the Money finder card in the Money Map Toolkit at the end of the guide and tick every way they think it earns.
steps.you: Write your own guess too, fold it up, and open both at the end. Don't hint.
ask: Who do you think pays the people who made it?
What would happen if nobody paid?
steps.tip: Something they love works best. They'll look harder at how it earns.

levels.explore: Pick it, and say who you think pays for it.
levels.develop: Tick every way on the Money finder card it might earn, and rank them by your guess.
levels.extend: Pick two things that do the same job, one free and one paid, and guess how the paid one manages with no ads.

steps.title: Collect the evidence
steps.why: A money map built on guesses is a story. Built on counts, it's a case.
steps.kid: Screen version: your kid watches you play a free game or a video site for 10 minutes and tallies every ad, buy button and 'watch an ad to' offer, using the Ad count card. Day-out version: they keep every receipt, photograph the price board and note what's sold at the exit, using the Day-out clues card.
steps.you: Hold the device yourself and keep purchases locked. Nobody taps an ad or a buy button. On a day out, hand them the receipts and let them ask staff one question.
ask: What was the first thing it tried to sell you?
Which ads were hardest to skip?
steps.tip: Notice where the shop is. If the only way out goes through it, that's evidence too.

levels.explore: Make a tally mark every time an ad appears while a parent plays.
levels.develop: Count for 10 minutes, time each ad, and work out minutes of ads per hour.
levels.extend: Compare the price of one thing inside, like a bottle of water, with the price at a store, and work out why people pay more there.

steps.title: Estimate the money
steps.why: Simple multiplying turns a pile of clues into a number you can argue about.
steps.kid: Your kid estimates one day's money, using the Money math card: people per day times what each spends. For a game, it's players times the share who buy times the price. They round, show every step and circle the number they trust least.
steps.you: Help find a starting number: a visitor count on a sign or website, or a guess from how busy it was. Ask 'Too high or too low?' about each one.
ask: Which number are you least sure of?
steps.tip: Round to easy numbers. 487 visitors becomes 500, and the math gets easy.

levels.explore: Count the people in one line or one room, and say if that's a lot.
levels.develop: Estimate one day's money for two ways it earns, and compare them.
levels.extend: The app store keeps about 30 cents of every dollar, or 15 for small makers. Take that out of your game estimate, then estimate one cost, like staff for a day.

steps.title: Draw the money map
steps.why: One page shows the whole business at a glance.
steps.kid: Your kid draws the thing in the middle of a page and every payer around it, using the Money map card: who pays, what for and roughly how much a day. Thicker arrows mean more money. Then they open the folded guesses from Step 1 and compare.
steps.you: Ask them to explain the map as if you'd never seen it. Ask about the thinnest arrow.
ask: Who pays without spending any money?
steps.tip: If people pay with their time or attention, give that an arrow too.

levels.explore: Draw the thing in the middle, and one arrow for each payer.
levels.develop: Draw the full map with thicker arrows for bigger money, and compare it with your guess.
levels.extend: Take one payer away, like the ads, and redraw the map to show what would have to change to keep it running.

steps.title: Plan your own money
steps.why: Once they can read how a business earns, they can choose how theirs will.
steps.kid: Your kid picks an idea of their own, like a stall, a game they'd design or a family event, and plans two ways it could earn, using the Your money plan card. They run each through the fair test, then draw its money map.
steps.you: Ask about the person paying: 'How would you feel paying that way?' Let them change the plan.
ask: Who pays in your plan, and for what?
Would you happily tell customers how you earn?
steps.tip: The best plans earn money in a way the customer is glad about.

levels.explore: Pick your idea, and choose one way it could make money.
levels.develop: Plan two ways it could earn, run the fair test, and draw the money map.
levels.extend: Design a version that's free for kids, and work out who else could pay so it still runs.

conclusion.headline: They know who pays for free.
conclusion.text: Wait for the next free thing that comes into the house, a new app or a free sample. If they ask 'So who's paying?' before you do, they're reading the world like a business owner.
conclusion.celebrate: When they explain their money map to someone, say: 'You counted it, you worked it out, and now you can see who pays.'
extensions: Make a money map for your library or a public park, and find out with a parent who pays for it
Watch a sports game together and count every sponsor's name you can see
Compare a paid app with no ads and its free version, and decide which you'd choose
Ask someone who runs a small business near you where their money comes from, and draw their map

signs: They ask 'Who pays for this?' about free things
They spot ads and buy buttons without being told
They estimate big numbers by multiplying small ones
makeItReal: Sit beside your kid with a timer and a pencil while you play their favourite free game, and count the ads together for 10 minutes.

classroom.intro: Kids are always surprised by who pays for free things, and a class investigation brings that out. You hold the device on the projector or plan a field trip, and groups collect evidence, estimate and draw money maps.

tips.d: Choose one free thing the whole class knows: a free game on the projector, a video site, or a museum, zoo or park on an upcoming field trip.
Play the free game or video site on your account at the front with purchases locked, following school device policy. Nobody taps an ad or a buy button; groups only tally.
Four jobs: an ad counter for the Ad count card, a timer, a price spotter and a map drawer. On a field trip, groups collect receipts and note what's sold at the exit.
Give groups a starting number, like the museum's posted visitor count or how many students are in the school, so the Money math card has something real to multiply.
A first money map has one arrow for each payer. Most groups draw the full map with thick and thin arrows, and some take one payer away and redraw what would have to change.
Post every group's map and open the folded guesses from Step 1. Students walk the gallery, find the thinnest arrow on each map and discuss which payer surprised them most.

classroom.timing: Three sessions of about 40 minutes cover guesses and evidence, estimating and the money map, then planning their own idea in Step 5. A field trip can be the evidence session. At home, students count ads while a grown-up plays a free game.
